content: Muscle cramps can occur in various parts of the body and may arise from numerous causes. Quinine has historically been used to treat muscle cramps regardless of their origin. However, its effectiveness and safety remain subjects of ongoing debate. This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of quinine-based treatments for muscle cramps. A systematic search was conducted on October 27, 2014, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Additional searches for ongoing trials were performed in November 2014. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants of all ages with muscle cramps of any cause or location, treated with quinine or its derivatives. Three independent reviewers selected studies for inclusion, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. Authors of the studies were contacted for supplementary information. For comparisons involving multiple trials, the quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE system. A total of 23 trials involving 1,586 participants were identified. Notably, 58% of the participants were from five unpublished studies. Quinine was compared to placebo in 20 trials (n = 1,140), vitamin E in four trials (n = 543), a quinine-vitamin E combination in three trials (n = 510), a quinine-theophylline combination in one trial (n = 77), and xylocaine injections into the gastrocnemius muscle in one trial (n = 24). The most frequently used quinine dosage was 300 mg/day, with a range of 200 to 500 mg/day. No new trials were identified in the 2014 update. The risk of bias varied significantly across the trials. While all 23 trials claimed to be randomized, only a minority adequately described their randomization and allocation concealment methods. Compared to placebo, quinine reduced the number of cramps over two weeks by 28%, cramp intensity by 10%, and the number of cramp days by 20%. However, quinine did not significantly affect cramp duration. Minor adverse events, primarily gastrointestinal symptoms, were more common with quinine than placebo (risk difference [RD] 3%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0% to 6%). Although quinine overdoses have been associated with potentially fatal adverse effects in other reports, the included trials did not show a significant difference in major adverse events compared to placebo (RD 0%, 95% CI -1% to 2%). One participant experienced thrombocytopenia while on quinine, corresponding to a 0.12% risk. When compared to other treatments, a quinine-vitamin E combination, vitamin E alone, and xylocaine injections into the gastrocnemius muscle showed no significant differences in outcomes, including adverse effects, when compared to quinine. In a single trial, a quinine-theophylline combination was found to be significantly more effective than quinine alone, though no significant differences in adverse events were observed. The authors concluded that there is low-quality evidence supporting the ability of quinine (200 to 500 mg daily) to significantly reduce the number of cramps and cramp days, and moderate-quality evidence that it reduces cramp intensity. Moderate-quality evidence also suggests that, when used for up to 60 days, quinine does not significantly increase the risk of serious adverse events compared to placebo. However, due to the potential for rare but fatal adverse events, quinine prescriptions are heavily restricted in some countries. Evidence from single trials suggests that combining theophylline with quinine may be more effective than quinine alone, while xylocaine injections into the gastrocnemius muscle are not significantly different from quinine in terms of outcomes. Lowto moderate-quality evidence indicates no significant differences between quinine and vitamin E or between quinine and a quinine-vitamin E combination. Further research is needed to explore alternative treatments, both pharmacological and non-pharmacological, for muscle cramps. Additional studies should investigate the optimal dosage and duration of quinine treatment, as well as measure serum quinine levels to establish a therapeutic range. Since serious adverse events are rare, large-scale population studies are required to better estimate their incidence. Future trials with longer follow-up periods are necessary to determine the duration of quinine's effects after discontinuation and to assess long-term adverse events. Continued exploration of new therapies is essential, and future studies should compare quinine with vitamin E, quinine-vitamin E combinations, and quinine-theophylline mixtures.
